 This is an Expo/React Native mobile application. Prioritize mobile-first patterns, performance, and cross-platform compatibility.
 
 # Pokedex+
 
 The Pokedex+ is an upgraded version of the pokedex. It is an index containing all the pokemon from every generation, including shinies. Every pokémon has a detail page. For people who want to get the best out of their pokemon.
 
 It runs on the PokeAPI (`https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/`)
 
 ## Commands
 
 Use `npx`
 
 ```bash
 npx expo install <package>  # ALWAYS use instead of npm/yarn/pnpm/bun add — resolves SDK-compatible versions
 npx expo start              # start the dev server
 npx expo lint               # lint
 npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck
 npx expo-doctor             # diagnose dependency and config issues
 npx expo install --fix      # fix incompatible package versions
 ```
 
 Run lint and typecheck before declaring any task done.
 
 ## Navigation & Routing
 
 - Use **Expo Router** for all navigation. Routes live in `src/app/` — every file there is a screen, `_layout.tsx` files define navigators. Keep non-route code (components, hooks, utils) outside `src/app/`.
 - Import `Link`, `router`, and `useLocalSearchParams` from `expo-router`.
 - Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction.md
 
 ## Building with EAS
 
 Use EAS to build, sign, and submit the app in the cloud (`eas build`, `eas submit`) and to ship over-the-air updates (`eas update`) — no local Xcode or Android Studio required. Run EAS CLI as `bunx eas-cli <command>` in Bun projects, or `npx eas-cli@latest <command>` otherwise; substitute that for bare `eas` in docs examples.
 Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/eas/index.md
 
 ## Rules
 
 - If `ios/` and `android/` directories do not exist, they are generated (Continuous Native Generation). Never create or edit them by hand — configure native behavior in `app.json` and config plugins.
 - Expo Go only includes its bundled native modules. After adding a library with native code, the app needs a development build: `npx expo run:ios|android` locally, or `eas build --profile development`.
 - Prefer recommended Expo modules over third-party libraries, and check your available skills before adding dependencies. Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/index.md
 - Follow the Figma design consistently across all screens and components.
 - Keep the alignment, positioning, and spacing of repeated UI elements consistent.
 
 ## Existing Project
 
 - Inspect the existing project before making changes.
 - Reuse existing components, hooks, utilities and architecture when needed.
 - Do not recreate working functionality when it's not needed.
 - Do not replace the existing application with a new project.
 - Explain significant architectural changes before implementing them.
 
 ## API
 
 - Use PokéAPI as the source of Pokémon data.
 - Follow the official PokéAPI documentation.
 - Understand the difference between `/pokemon/` and `/pokemon-species/`.
 - Fetch additional Pokémon data only when needed.
 - Handle API failures, missing data and unavailable sprites.
 - Do not assume optional API fields are always populated.
 - Avoid unnecessary API requests and duplicate data fetching.
 
 ## Database
 
 - Use SQLite for persistent local data.
 - Follow the database structure defined in the project specifications.
 - Keep Pokémon API data separate from user-specific data such as Favorites.
 - Use database migrations when changing an existing database structure.
 - Do not store information locally if it can be derived reliably from existing data.
 
 ## Code Quality
 
 - Reuse the code language from existing project.
 - Prefer reusable components and hooks.
 - Keep components focused on a single responsibility.
 - Use meaningful, adhd/asd-friendly variable and function names, but don't make it too long.
 - Add adhd/asd-friendly comments when they explain non-obvious logic or important decisions.
 - Do not add comments that simply repeat what the code already says.
 - Avoid unnecessary dependencies.
 - When implementing a feature, explain the important parts of the implementation in plain language. Explain what the code does, how the components work together, and why important technical decisions were made. Do not explain every line unless asked.

 # Pokémon Catching Simulator
 
 ## Context
 
 - The simulator screen is `src/app/pokemon/simulator/[id].tsx`; it opens from the selected Pokémon's detail page.
 - Pokémon species data, including its base capture rate, comes from PokeAPI `/pokemon-species/{id}`. Game appearances come from `/pokemon/{id}`; item-category endpoints are listed in `specs/product.md`.
 - The simulator uses Poké Balls from item categories 33 and 34.
 - Use the existing theme in `src/constants/theme.ts`, the Rubik font files in `assets/fonts`, and no new dependencies.
 
 ## Goals
 
 - Show how a selected Poké Ball and catch conditions affect a Pokémon's chance of being caught under an applicable game's rules.
 - Let the user try repeated simulated throws without saving caught Pokémon.
 
 ## Requirements
 
 ### Pokémon and game rules
 
 - Open the simulator for the Pokémon selected on the detail page.
 - Show the Pokémon's name, Pokédex ID, and the same form and regular or shiny sprite selected on the detail page.
 - Use the selected Pokémon's PokeAPI `/pokemon/{id}` `game_indices` to determine its appearances. Consider main-series games and remakes only; exclude side games.
 - Group games only when their catch behavior is identical, including all Poké Ball effects and condition effects. Offer only rulesets that apply to the selected Pokémon, and list the applicable game titles in the ruleset's concise, plain-language explanation.
 - Do not offer a ruleset unless its catch behavior can be calculated accurately. Do not show mathematical formulas or use an estimate instead.
 - Select the ruleset containing the newest applicable game by release order. Let the user choose another available ruleset; changing it recalculates the catch chance.
 - If no accurate ruleset applies to the selected Pokémon, explain that no game-accurate ruleset is available and disable “Throw Ball”.
 
 ### Poké Balls and catch conditions
 
 - Load all Poké Balls in item categories 33 and 34. For each ball, show its name, PokeAPI ID, and description. Keep balls unavailable in the selected ruleset visible but disabled with an explanation. Start with a standard Poké Ball selected when it is available.
 - Let the user change the Pokémon's remaining HP using a 0–100% slider that starts at 100%.
 - Let the user choose “No status”, Sleep, Freeze, Paralysis, Burn, or Poison. Start with “No status” selected.
 - Provide controls for time of day and separate on/off settings for whether the encounter is in water and whether the Pokémon is being fished. Offer time choices used by the selected ruleset. Start with Day selected when available, otherwise the first time choice; start with water and fishing both off.
 - Apply only conditions relevant to the selected ball and ruleset.
 - Calculate and show the actual per-throw catch chance as a percentage using the species' base capture rate and the selected ruleset's game behavior for the current Pokémon, ball, and conditions. Do not display mathematical formulas.
 
 ### Throw results
 
 - The “Throw Ball” action simulates one throw using the displayed catch chance.
 - Show an animation and a clear caught or escaped result.
 - After either result, let the user throw again or change the settings. Keep the current settings until the user changes them.
 - Do not save or otherwise add caught Pokémon to the user's data.
 
 ### Loading, errors, and visual design
 
 - Show loading and retryable error states for Pokémon data and Poké Ball data independently.
 - Use the app's Rubik font, loaded with Expo Font from `assets/fonts`.
 - Use the app's theme colors and spacing from `src/constants/theme.ts`.
 
 ## Acceptance Criteria
 
 - [ ] Opening the simulator shows the selected Pokémon's name, ID, form, and selected regular or shiny sprite.
 - [ ] Only applicable main-series games and remakes in the selected Pokémon's PokeAPI `game_indices` contribute rulesets. Games share a named ruleset only when their full catch behavior, including every ball and condition effect, is identical. The ruleset explanation names its applicable games and describes the effect in plain language without a formula.
 - [ ] The ruleset containing the newest applicable game is selected by default; the user can choose another applicable ruleset and the catch chance updates to that game's behavior. If no accurate ruleset applies, the screen explains this and disables “Throw Ball”.
 - [ ] The simulator lists the Poké Balls from both specified item categories with each ball's name, ID, and description. Balls unavailable in the selected ruleset remain visible but disabled with an explanation. A standard Poké Ball is selected by default when available.
 - [ ] The user can set remaining HP with a 0–100% slider, select any specified status condition, and set time of day and separate water and fishing controls. Initial values are 100% HP, “No status”, both water and fishing off, and Day or the first available time choice. Time choices match the selected ruleset.
 - [ ] The displayed percentage is the actual chance of catching the selected Pokémon with one throw under the selected ruleset, ball, and relevant conditions; no formula or estimate is shown.
 - [ ] Each throw shows an animated caught or escaped result; the user can retry or change settings, and caught Pokémon are not saved.
 - [ ] Pokémon and Poké Ball data each show loading, retryable error, and successful states; the screen uses the Rubik font and theme.
 
 ## Out of Scope
 
 - Saving caught Pokémon.
 - Simulating Pokémon battles.
 - Side games and estimated catch results.

 # Pokedex+
 
 The Pokedex+ is an upgraded version of the pokedex. It is an index containing all the pokemon from every generation, including shinies. Every pokémon has a detail page. For people who want to get the best out of their pokemon.
 
 ## Core action
 
 Pick a pokémon and see it's information
 
 ## Features
 
 <One line per feature, linking to its file in `specs/features/`. 3 to 6, not
 more. Each one becomes a GitHub issue.>
 
 1. [Normal list](./features/pokédex-index.md) Browse an index of normal pokémon
 2. [Search by name](./features/pokédex-search.md) Search pokémon by name
 3. [Pokémon detail](./features/pokédex-detail.md) See general info, stats, and evolution of a pokémon
 4. [Favorites list](./features/pokédex-favorites.md) Browse an index of shiny pokémon
 5. [Pokémon Comparison] (./features/pokédex-compare.md) Put two Pokémon side by side and sees who is stronger on which stat.
 6. [Catching-simulator] (./features/pokédex-simulator.md) Simulate catching a pokémon (in multiple conditions) with a list of usable pokéballs.
 
 ## Data
 
 - **API**: PokeApi, no login, no key
 - **Endpoints**:
   /pokemon?limit=2000 — Fetch the complete Pokémon index.
   /pokemon/{id or name} — Fetch Pokémon information, including stats, types and sprites.
   /pokemon-species/{id} — Fetch species information and evolution-chain URL.
   /item-category/33/ — Fetch special balls
   /item-category/34/ — Fetch standard balls
 - **Stored on the phone**:
   Table pokemon in SQLite: id (PokéAPI Pokémon resource ID), species_id (PokéAPI species ID), name, height, weight, base_experience, types_json, abilities_json, stats_json, sprites_json, forms_json, generation, capture_rate, updated_at. Each base Pokémon and each listed regional, Mega, or Gigantamax variant is a separate row with its own Pokémon resource ID. `forms_json` stores related form metadata, including Pokémon resource IDs and available regular/shiny sprite references.
   Table personal_list: personal_list_id, pokemon_id (PokéAPI Pokémon resource ID), created_at. Each variant can be favorited independently.
 
 ## Technical choices
 
 <Fill in the two below: every app makes these choices. For each one: what
 you picked, what else you could have done, and why. Write it before you
 build. If you change your mind later, change it here too.>
 
 - **Stored in SQLite**: It allows for local, persistent storage and structured queries, which is similar to SQL and I am more familiar with. I don't have enough knowledge about AsyncStorage.
 - **Native feature**: Share on your favorites tab. Share your favorite pokémon with your friends.
 
 ## Technical core
 
 <Tick these off as you build. They are required for a pass.>
 
 - [ ] Runs in Expo Go
 - [ ] Live data through TanStack Query
 - [ ] At least 2 screens with Expo Router
 - [ ] Something in SQLite that survives a restart
 - [ ] Loading and error state on every load
 - [ ] One native feature: Share favorites, in the favorites tab
 - [ ] TypeScript and ESLint without errors
 - [ ] UI, data and logic in separate files
 
 ## Optional
 
 <Tick the ones you built, +0.5 each. Delete the rest or leave them unticked.>
 
 - [ ] Three different Reanimated animations, each with a purpose
 - [ ] Dark mode: every screen looks right, all colours from the theme
 - [ ] Pagination: page by page while you scroll, not all at once
 - [ ] Clean TypeScript: no `any`, no `as` casts, no `@ts-ignore`
 - [ ] Design (not Pokédex): a consistent own style with your own font
 - [ ] Localization: two languages
 - [ ] No warnings: no `console.log`, none in the terminal or on screen
 - [ ] Tests: one per feature on the logic, `npm test` passes
 - [ ] CI: lint and tsc on every push
 - [ ] Accessibility: button labels, largest text size
 - [ ] Optimistic update
 
 ## Out of scope
 
 accounts

 # Implementation Plan: Pokémon Detail Page
 
 Issue: [Kuhloud/Pokedex#3](https://github.com/Kuhloud/Pokedex/issues/3)
 
 ## Scope and design baseline
 
 Follow `specs/features/pokedex-detail.md` and the referenced list, Favorites, product, and simulator specifications. Use the user-provided detail screenshots as the visual baseline: a pale blue Pokémon header, overlapping sprite, favorite control, and About/Stats/Evolution tabs. The written specs take precedence where they require controls or information not shown in the screenshots. Use the existing theme, Rubik font, and no new dependencies.
 
 The only detail screen source path named by the feature spec is `src/app/pokemon/[id].tsx`. The spec also names the simulator destination `src/app/pokemon/simulator/[id].tsx`; its behavior is separately specified and is not part of this implementation. Before opening or changing any other source file not named in the relevant specs, identify the exact file and reason and ask the user for permission. Do not modify list, database, shared API, navigation, or other implementation files without that permission.
 
 The user approved inspecting `package.json` and `src/hooks/use-pokemon-list.ts`, then inspecting and modifying `src/services/pokemon-api.ts` to provide the required detail and evolution data. The existing simulator route had no default export; the user approved adding only a minimal placeholder at the spec-named destination so Catch navigation works. Simulator behavior remains out of scope.
 
 ## Status
 
 Implemented and verified. The requested detail flow is complete; the simulator destination is intentionally only a placeholder.
 
 ## Implementation plan
 
 1. After plan approval, inspect the specified detail screen and only the other source files explicitly identified by the applicable specs. Confirm how existing API, theme, font, favorites, and list-selection behavior can be reused without expanding file scope.
 2. If the required behavior depends on an unspecified source file, pause and ask permission to inspect and, if necessary, modify that exact file before proceeding.
 3. Implement the detail header with the selected Pokémon's name, Pokédex ID, type badges, selected-form regular/shiny sprite, back navigation, Favorite control, and Catch navigation. Keep form selection independent from shiny selection; offer only the regional forms specified by the list feature and show the shiny control only when that form has a shiny sprite.
 4. Add About, Stats, and Evolution tabs, with About selected initially and a clear selected-tab indicator. Show all About fields and missing-value fallbacks; show the six stats with bars scaled against the fixed 0–255 range.
 5. Load the complete evolution family independently from primary detail data. Render all branches, available Mega forms, card sprites/names/IDs, gender-differentiated sprite details where applicable, and an accent highlight for the selected Pokémon. Make other family cards navigable and render a single self-card for a Pokémon without other evolutionary forms.
 6. Preserve the latest form and regular/shiny selections when navigating back to the list. Provide independent loading/error/retry states for detail data and evolution-family data, and a neutral sprite placeholder when needed.
 
 ## Suggestions and decisions to confirm during implementation
 
 - The screenshots show a compact top header that scrolls away while the tab content remains visible. Preserve that feel on smaller screens while ensuring the tabs and content remain usable; avoid making the Pokémon artwork obscure controls.
 - The screenshots show only a subset of the required controls. Keep the spec-required form/shiny selection, Favorite, and Catch actions discoverable without sacrificing the visual hierarchy.
 - PokeAPI evolution-chain data may not represent every Mega form as a normal evolution species. Include Mega forms only when they are present in available API data, as the spec requests; if the API shape or an existing data helper cannot support this without out-of-spec files, pause and ask before expanding scope.
 
 ## Task checklist
 
 - [x] Inspect the explicitly specified detail route and the applicable feature specs after plan approval.
 - [x] Ask permission before inspecting or changing any source files not named in the specs.
 - [x] Build the detail header and selected-form regular/shiny controls, preserving selections when returning to the list.
 - [x] Implement Favorite persistence and Catch navigation using the specified existing behavior and destinations.
 - [x] Add About, Stats, and Evolution tabs with all specified fields, visuals, navigation, and empty/fallback states.
 - [x] Load and render the complete available evolution family independently, including branches and available Mega forms.
 - [x] Add detail and evolution loading, retryable error, missing-value, and missing-sprite states.
 - [x] Match the attached mobile design using the existing theme and Rubik font without adding dependencies.
 - [x] Validate the required behavior and run lint and TypeScript checks.

`expo-font` allows loading fonts from the web and using them in React Native components. See more detailed usage information in the [Fonts](https://docs.expo.dev/develop/user-interface/fonts.md) guide.

## Installation

```sh
# npm
npx expo install expo-font

# yarn
yarn expo install expo-font

# pnpm
pnpm expo install expo-font

# bun
bun expo install expo-font
```

If you are installing this in an [existing React Native app](https://docs.expo.dev/bare/overview.md), make sure to [install `expo`](https://docs.expo.dev/bare/installing-expo-modules.md) in your project.

## Configuration in app config

There are two ways to add fonts to your app: using the `expo-font` config plugin (recommended for Android and iOS) or loading them at runtime (which works across all platforms including web).

On Android and iOS, the plugin allows you to embed font files at build time which is more efficient than [`useFonts`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v58.0.0/sdk/font.md#usefonts) or [`loadAsync`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v58.0.0/sdk/font.md#loadasyncfontfamilyorfontmap-source). After you set up the config plugin and run [prebuild](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/continuous-native-generation.md#usage), you can render custom fonts right away. The plugin can be configured in different ways, see the [Fonts](https://docs.expo.dev/develop/user-interface/fonts.md#with-expo-font-config-plugin) guide on how to use it.

### Example app.json with config plugin

```json app.json
{
  "expo": {
    "plugins": [
      [
        "expo-font",
        {
          "fonts": ["./path/to/file.ttf"],
          "android": {
            "fonts": [
              {
                "fontFamily": "Source Serif 4",
                "fontDefinitions": [
                  {
                    "path": "./path/to/SourceSerif4-ExtraBold.ttf",
                    "weight": 800
                  }
                ]
              },
              {
                "fontFamily": "Roboto Flex",
                "path": "./path/to/RobotoFlex.ttf",
                "fontDefinitions": [
                  { "weight": 400 },
                  { "weight": 700 },
                  { "weight": 400, "style": "italic", "axes": { "slnt": -10 } }
                ]
              }
            ]
          },
          "ios": {
            "fonts": ["./path/to/SourceSerif4-ExtraBold.ttf"]
          }
        }
      ]
    ]
  }
}
```

### Configurable properties

| Name | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fonts` | `[]` | An array of font definitions to link to the native project. The paths should be relative to the project root. On Android, the file name becomes the font family name. On iOS, the font family name is always taken directly from the font file and may not be the same as the file name — follow the [naming advice](https://docs.expo.dev/develop/user-interface/fonts.md#how-to-determine-which-font-family-name-to-use) or use [`getLoadedFonts`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v58.0.0/sdk/font.md#getloadedfonts) to see what fonts are available. |
| `android` | `{}` | An object with a `fonts` array of font definitions to link to the native project on Android. Use the object syntax within `fonts` to embed [xml fonts](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/text-and-emoji/fonts-in-xml) with custom family name. |
| `ios` | `{}` | An object with a `fonts` array of font file paths to link to the native project on iOS. The font family name is taken directly from the font file. |

#### Are you using this library in an existing React Native app?

-   **Android:** Copy font files to **android/app/src/main/assets/fonts**.
-   **iOS**: See [Adding a Custom Font to Your App](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/adding-a-custom-font-to-your-app) in the Apple Developer documentation.

_Catch redirects here. For the concept of catching a Pokémon, see [Caught Pokémon](/wiki/Caught_Pok%C3%A9mon "Caught Pokémon")._

* * *

Each [species of Pokémon](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_\(species\) "Pokémon (species)") has a **catch rate** that applies to all its members. When a [Poké Ball](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball "Poké Ball") is thrown at a wild Pokémon, the game uses that Pokémon's catch rate in a formula to determine the chances of [catching](/wiki/Caught_Pok%C3%A9mon "Caught Pokémon") that Pokémon. Higher catch rates mean that the Pokémon is easier to catch, up to a maximum of 255. The formula also takes into account the following factors: 

*   The health of the Pokémon (relative to its full health)
*   The type of [Poké Ball](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball "Poké Ball")
*   Any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") of the wild Pokémon
*   Any active [Pass Powers](/wiki/Entralink#Pass_Powers "Entralink") (in [Generation V](/wiki/Generation_V "Generation V")), [O-Powers](/wiki/O-Power "O-Power") (in [Generation VI](/wiki/Generation_VI "Generation VI")), [Rotom Powers](/wiki/Rotom_Pok%C3%A9dex#Rotom_Powers "Rotom Pokédex") (in [Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Ultra_Sun_and_Ultra_Moon "Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon")) or [Meal Powers](/wiki/Sandwich#Meal_Powers "Sandwich") (in [Pokémon Scarlet and Violet](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Scarlet_and_Violet "Pokémon Scarlet and Violet"))

Certain other factors, such as the target Pokémon's level, may also factor in depending on the type of Poké Ball used or the generation. 

Circumstances where capture is guaranteed—i.e. using the [Master Ball](/wiki/Master_Ball "Master Ball") and [Park Ball](/wiki/Park_Ball "Park Ball"), any Poké Ball used on [Kalos Route 2](/wiki/Kalos_Route_2 "Kalos Route 2")**[XY](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_X_and_Y "Pokémon X and Y")**, [Route 101](/wiki/Hoenn_Route_101 "Hoenn Route 101")**[ORAS](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Omega_Ruby_and_Alpha_Sapphire "Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire")**, [Alola Route 1](/wiki/Alola_Route_1 "Alola Route 1") prior to the start of the festival in [Iki Town](/wiki/Iki_Town "Iki Town")**[SM](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Sun_and_Moon "Pokémon Sun and Moon")[USUM](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Ultra_Sun_and_Ultra_Moon "Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon")**, in the [Entree Forest](/wiki/Entralink "Entralink"), in hosted non-event [Max Raid Battles](/wiki/Max_Raid_Battle "Max Raid Battle"), or any [Tera Raid Battle](/wiki/Tera_Raid_Battle "Tera Raid Battle")—bypass the catching formula entirely. Circumstances where capture is impossible (e.g. against [unidentified ghosts](/wiki/Ghost_\(Pok%C3%A9mon_Tower\) "Ghost (Pokémon Tower)") in the [Pokémon Tower](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Tower "Pokémon Tower")) also bypass the capture formula and prevent capture even if the ball used would otherwise guarantee capture.

* * *

[![](https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/3/3e/Pok%C3%A9_Balls.png/250px-Pok%C3%A9_Balls.png)](/wiki/File:Pok%C3%A9_Balls.png)

The 28 Poké Ball variants found in the [core series](/wiki/Core_series "Core series") (excluding those exclusive to Pokémon Legends: Arceus)

[![](https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/2/2d/Pok%C3%A9_Ball_sketch.png/250px-Pok%C3%A9_Ball_sketch.png)](/wiki/File:Pok%C3%A9_Ball_sketch.png)

Original concept

A **Poké Ball** (Japanese: **モンスターボール** _Monster Ball_) is a type of [item](/wiki/Item "Item") that is critical to a [Trainer](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trainer "Pokémon Trainer")'s quest, used for [catching](/wiki/Caught_Pok%C3%A9mon "Caught Pokémon") and storing [Pokémon](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_\(species\) "Pokémon (species)"). Both a general term used to describe the various kinds as well as a specific term to refer to the most basic among these variations, Poké Balls are ubiquitous in the modern [Pokémon world](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_world "Pokémon world"). 

Up to six Pokémon can be carried with a [Trainer](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trainer "Pokémon Trainer") in Poké Balls, while more Poké Balls can be held in the [Bag](/wiki/Bag "Bag") for later use. These six Pokémon in the Poké Balls can be attached to the user's belt for carrying them around. Some Pokémon do not like to be carried around in Poké Balls, such as [Ash's Pikachu](/wiki/Ash%27s_Pikachu "Ash's Pikachu").

The headgear of the protagonists of [Kanto](/wiki/Kanto "Kanto"), [Hoenn](/wiki/Hoenn "Hoenn"), [Sinnoh](/wiki/Sinnoh "Sinnoh"), and [Unova](/wiki/Unova "Unova")-based games feature Poké Ball designs, as do the [Bags](/wiki/Bag "Bag") of the protagonists of [Johto](/wiki/Johto "Johto")-based games.  ## Capture method (Generation I)
 
 The capture method in [Generation I](/wiki/Generation_I "Generation I") differs significantly from those of later generations. To determine whether a Pokémon is caught or not, the steps below are performed. If, at any point, the Pokémon is caught or breaks free, the steps following that point are not performed. 
 
 1.  If a [Master Ball](/wiki/Master_Ball "Master Ball") is used, the Pokémon is **caught**.
 2.  Generate a random number, _N_, depending on the type of ball used.
     *   For a [Poké Ball](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball_\(item\) "Poké Ball (item)"): 0 to 255.
     *   For a [Great Ball](/wiki/Great_Ball "Great Ball"): 0 to 200.
     *   Otherwise ([Ultra Ball](/wiki/Ultra_Ball "Ultra Ball") or [Safari Ball](/wiki/Safari_Ball "Safari Ball")): 0 to 150.
 3.  The Pokémon is **caught** if...
     *   It is asleep or frozen and _N_ is less than 25.
     *   It is paralyzed, burned, or poisoned and _N_ is less than 12.
 4.  Otherwise, if _N_ minus the status threshold (above) is greater than the Pokémon's catch rate, the Pokémon **breaks free**.
 5.  If not, generate a random value, _M_, between 0 and 255.
 6.  Calculate _f_:
     *   f\=⌊HPmax×255×4HPcurrent×Ball⌋, where the value of Ball is 8 if a Great Ball is used or 12 otherwise. The minimum value of _f_ is 1 and its maximum value is 255.
 7.  If _f_ is greater than or equal to _M_, the Pokémon is **caught**. Otherwise, the Pokémon **breaks free**. In practical terms, lowering the target's HP to 1/3 of its maximum will guarantee capture with a Poké Ball, while lowering it to 1/2 will guarantee capture with a Great Ball.
 
 If the Pokémon broke free, the steps below are performed to determine how many times the ball will shake. 
 
 1.  Calculate _d_:
     *   d\=⌊catchRate×100Ball⌋, where the value of Ball is 255 for the Poké Ball, 200 for the Great Ball, or 150 for other balls.
 2.  If _d_ is greater than or equal to 256, the ball shakes three times before the Pokémon breaks free.
 3.  If not, calculate x\=⌊d×f255⌋+s, where _s_ is 10 if the Pokémon is asleep or frozen, 5 if it is paralyzed, poisoned, or burned, or 0 otherwise.
 4.  If...
     *   _x_ < 10: the Ball misses the Pokémon completely.
     *   _x_ < 30: the Ball shakes once before the Pokémon breaks free.
     *   _x_ < 70: the Ball shakes twice before the Pokémon breaks free.
     *   Otherwise, the Ball shakes three times before the Pokémon breaks free.
 
 This algorithm thus has several unique properties that do not apply in later generations: 
 
 *   The number of times a Poké Ball shakes before failing to catch a Pokémon is a rough approximation of the Pokémon's catch odds.
 *   If a Pokémon will break free, a given combination of ball plus status condition plus HP will always result in the same number of shakes. This means that, if a given number of shakes is observed before the Pokémon breaks free for a given combination of these values, if the ball is ever observed to shake more times with the same combination of values, the Pokémon will be caught.

 *   Due to the nature of the algorithm, Ultra Balls will only perform better than Great Balls on Pokémon whose capture rates are above 55 and below 200 in Generation I. Ultra Balls increase the overall chance of capture by as much as 20% in comparison to Great Balls for Pokémon near the center of that range.

 ### Approximate probability
 
 The following calculation will give the exact probability of catching a Pokémon whose catch rate is at most a specific value. It will give results which are too high if the catch rates are more than this, but it remains a useful approximation. Specifically: 
 
 *   For a Poké Ball, it is exact for Pokémon with a catch rate of at most 230;
 *   For a Great Ball, it is exact for Pokémon with a catch rate of at most 175
 *   For an Ultra or Safari Ball, it is exact for Pokémon with a catch rate of at most 125.
 
 CaptureProbability≈statusConditionBall+1+(catchRate+1Ball+1×f+1256) 
 
 where 
 
 *   statusCondition\={12,if poisoned, burned, or paralyzed25,if frozen or asleep0,otherwise
 *   Ball\={255,if using a Poké Ball200,if using a Great Ball150,otherwise
 *   _f_ is defined in the above section for the capture method.
 *   _catchRate_ (given as an integer value) is stated on each individual Pokémon's article.
 
 ### Safari Game
 
 The Safari Game has additional mechanics exclusive to the [Safari Zone](/wiki/Kanto_Safari_Zone "Kanto Safari Zone"); these modify the Pokémon's catch rate before any other multipliers: 
 
 *   If bait is thrown, the Pokémon's catch rate is halved (and rounded down), a random "eating counter" between 1 and 5 is generated, and any "angry counter" is reset;
 *   If a rock is thrown, the Pokémon's catch rate is doubled and a random "angry counter" between 1 and 5 is generated, and any "eating counter" is reset.
 
 At the end of every turn, the counters are decreased by one. If the "angry counter" hits zero, the Pokémon's catch rate is reset.

# General capture method (Generation II onwards)

The capture algorithms in [Generation II](/wiki/Generation_II "Generation II") and onwards have three essential components: the modified catch rate, the "shake probability", and the "shake checks". Generation II handles shake checks slightly differently than the later generations. 

### Modified catch rate

The modified catch rate, _a_, is the catch rate after various factors such as weakening the Pokémon and using stronger Poké Balls are taken into consideration. A modified catch rate may never fall to 0 (that is, render a Pokémon impossible to capture), but it may cause the modified rate to fall below its original unmodified catch rate (such as from high health, Heavy Balls, Baiting in the [Safari Zone](/wiki/Safari_Zone "Safari Zone"), or the dark grass penalty in [Generation V](/wiki/Generation_V "Generation V")). In [Generation III](/wiki/Generation_III "Generation III") and [Generation IV](/wiki/Generation_IV "Generation IV"), the modified catch rate may never fall below 1. 

### Shake probability

The shake probability, _b_, is a value that determines the probability that a single shake check passes. 

### Shake checks

Shake checks are performed to determine whether the Pokémon will be caught or, if the Pokémon breaks free, the number of shakes that will occur before it does so. 

In Generation II, whether a Pokémon will be caught is determined before any shake checks are performed, and shake checks are only performed if the Pokémon is not caught. 

## Capture method (Generation II)

### Modified catch rate

The modified catch rate _a_ is calculated in [Generation II](/wiki/Generation_II "Generation II") as follows: 

a\=max⁡(⌊(3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent)×ratemodified3×HPmax⌋,1)+bonusstatus 

where 

*   HPmax is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at full health,
*   HPcurrent is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at the moment,
*   ratemodified is the catch rate of the Pokémon modified by the ball used, but no less than 1 and no more than 255,
*   bonusstatus is the modifier for any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") the Pokémon has (10 for sleep or freeze, 0 otherwise).
    *   bonusstatus was intended to equal 5 for paralyze, poison, or burn, but due to a glitch, the game skips this check.

If 3 × HPmax > 255, then both 3 × HPmax and 2 × HPcurrent are halved twice (and rounded down after each division) for use in the formula, as the values used are unsigned 8-bit integers. If the latter product is 0, it is set to 1 instead. 

If the Pokémon's HP is 342 or greater, the 3 × HPmax value will be truncated and the subtraction may underflow, giving bizarre results and even making it possible for the game to freeze; however, no such Pokémon can be legitimately encountered in-game. 

_a_ is capped at 255. 

The Apricorn balls apply changes directly to the Pokémon's catch rate, but due to various glitches, many of them do not work as intended. These balls were fixed for Generation IV. 

### Shake probability

The shake probability _b_ is determined from the table below, depending on the value of _a_.

| --- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 63  | 75 | 84 | 90 | 95 | 103 | 113 | 126 | 134 | 149 | 160 | 169 | 177 | 191 | 201 | 211 | 220 | 227 | 234 | 240 | 246 | 251 | 253 | 255 |

### Shake checks

First, a check is performed to determine whether the Pokémon is caught at all. A random number between 0 and 255 is generated, and if this number is less than or equal to _a_, the Pokémon is caught. 

Shake checks are only performed if the Pokémon is not caught. A single shake check consists of generating a random number between 0 and 255 and comparing it to _b_. This is done at most three times, but if the number generated in a given shake check is greater than or equal to _b_, no further shake checks will be performed. The number of times the ball shakes is the same as the number of shake checks that were performed. The table is essentially a very low-precision lookup table with numbers corresponding to the shake rate in later generations, so ultimately, aside from rounding errors (very bad ones in this case), the shake and capture rate remain similar between Generation II and the formula later used in Generation III.

_Catch redirects here. For the concept of catching a Pokémon, see [Caught Pokémon](/wiki/Caught_Pok%C3%A9mon "Caught Pokémon")._

* * *

Each [species of Pokémon](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_\(species\) "Pokémon (species)") has a **catch rate** that applies to all its members. When a [Poké Ball](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball "Poké Ball") is thrown at a wild Pokémon, the game uses that Pokémon's catch rate in a formula to determine the chances of [catching](/wiki/Caught_Pok%C3%A9mon "Caught Pokémon") that Pokémon. Higher catch rates mean that the Pokémon is easier to catch, up to a maximum of 255. The formula also takes into account the following factors: 

*   The health of the Pokémon (relative to its full health)
*   The type of [Poké Ball](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball "Poké Ball")
*   Any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") of the wild Pokémon
*   Any active [Pass Powers](/wiki/Entralink#Pass_Powers "Entralink") (in [Generation V](/wiki/Generation_V "Generation V")), [O-Powers](/wiki/O-Power "O-Power") (in [Generation VI](/wiki/Generation_VI "Generation VI")), [Rotom Powers](/wiki/Rotom_Pok%C3%A9dex#Rotom_Powers "Rotom Pokédex") (in [Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Ultra_Sun_and_Ultra_Moon "Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon")) or [Meal Powers](/wiki/Sandwich#Meal_Powers "Sandwich") (in [Pokémon Scarlet and Violet](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Scarlet_and_Violet "Pokémon Scarlet and Violet"))

Certain other factors, such as the target Pokémon's level, may also factor in depending on the type of Poké Ball used or the generation. 

Circumstances where capture is guaranteed—i.e. using the [Master Ball](/wiki/Master_Ball "Master Ball") and [Park Ball](/wiki/Park_Ball "Park Ball"), any Poké Ball used on [Kalos Route 2](/wiki/Kalos_Route_2 "Kalos Route 2")**[XY](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_X_and_Y "Pokémon X and Y")**, [Route 101](/wiki/Hoenn_Route_101 "Hoenn Route 101")**[ORAS](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Omega_Ruby_and_Alpha_Sapphire "Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire")**, [Alola Route 1](/wiki/Alola_Route_1 "Alola Route 1") prior to the start of the festival in [Iki Town](/wiki/Iki_Town "Iki Town")**[SM](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Sun_and_Moon "Pokémon Sun and Moon")[USUM](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Ultra_Sun_and_Ultra_Moon "Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon")**, in the [Entree Forest](/wiki/Entralink "Entralink"), in hosted non-event [Max Raid Battles](/wiki/Max_Raid_Battle "Max Raid Battle"), or any [Tera Raid Battle](/wiki/Tera_Raid_Battle "Tera Raid Battle")—bypass the catching formula entirely. Circumstances where capture is impossible (e.g. against [unidentified ghosts](/wiki/Ghost_\(Pok%C3%A9mon_Tower\) "Ghost (Pokémon Tower)") in the [Pokémon Tower](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Tower "Pokémon Tower")) also bypass the capture formula and prevent capture even if the ball used would otherwise guarantee capture.

 Contents of https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Catch_rate:
 # General capture method (Generation II onwards)
 
 The capture algorithms in [Generation II](/wiki/Generation_II "Generation II") and onwards have three essential components: the modified catch rate, the "shake probability", and the "shake checks". Generation II handles shake checks slightly differently than the later generations. 
 
 ### Modified catch rate
 
 The modified catch rate, _a_, is the catch rate after various factors such as weakening the Pokémon and using stronger Poké Balls are taken into consideration. A modified catch rate may never fall to 0 (that is, render a Pokémon impossible to capture), but it may cause the modified rate to fall below its original unmodified catch rate (such as from high health, Heavy Balls, Baiting in the [Safari Zone](/wiki/Safari_Zone "Safari Zone"), or the dark grass penalty in [Generation V](/wiki/Generation_V "Generation V")). In [Generation III](/wiki/Generation_III "Generation III") and [Generation IV](/wiki/Generation_IV "Generation IV"), the modified catch rate may never fall below 1. 
 
 ### Shake probability
 
 The shake probability, _b_, is a value that determines the probability that a single shake check passes. 
 
 ### Shake checks
 
 Shake checks are performed to determine whether the Pokémon will be caught or, if the Pokémon breaks free, the number of shakes that will occur before it does so. 
 
 In Generation II, whether a Pokémon will be caught is determined before any shake checks are performed, and shake checks are only performed if the Pokémon is not caught. 
 
 ## Capture method (Generation II)
 
 ### Modified catch rate
 
 The modified catch rate _a_ is calculated in [Generation II](/wiki/Generation_II "Generation II") as follows: 
 
 a\=max⁡(⌊(3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent)×ratemodified3×HPmax⌋,1)+bonusstatus 
 
 where 
 
 *   HPmax is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at full health,
 *   HPcurrent is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at the moment,
 *   ratemodified is the catch rate of the Pokémon modified by the ball used, but no less than 1 and no more than 255,
 *   bonusstatus is the modifier for any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") the Pokémon has (10 for sleep or freeze, 0 otherwise).
     *   bonusstatus was intended to equal 5 for paralyze, poison, or burn, but due to a glitch, the game skips this check.
 
 If 3 × HPmax > 255, then both 3 × HPmax and 2 × HPcurrent are halved twice (and rounded down after each division) for use in the formula, as the values used are unsigned 8-bit integers. If the latter product is 0, it is set to 1 instead. 
 
 If the Pokémon's HP is 342 or greater, the 3 × HPmax value will be truncated and the subtraction may underflow, giving bizarre results and even making it possible for the game to freeze; however, no such Pokémon can be legitimately encountered in-game. 
 
 _a_ is capped at 255. 
 
 The Apricorn balls apply changes directly to the Pokémon's catch rate, but due to various glitches, many of them do not work as intended. These balls were fixed for Generation IV. 
 
 ### Shake probability
 
 The shake probability _b_ is determined from the table below, depending on the value of _a_. 
 
 | _a_ |    |    |    |    |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |
 | --- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
 | 63  | 75 | 84 | 90 | 95 | 103 | 113 | 126 | 134 | 149 | 160 | 169 | 177 | 191 | 201 | 211 | 220 | 227 | 234 | 240 | 246 | 251 | 253 | 255 |
 
 ### Shake checks
 
 First, a check is performed to determine whether the Pokémon is caught at all. A random number between 0 and 255 is generated, and if this number is less than or equal to _a_, the Pokémon is caught. 
 
 Shake checks are only performed if the Pokémon is not caught. A single shake check consists of generating a random number between 0 and 255 and comparing it to _b_. This is done at most three times, but if the number generated in a given shake check is greater than or equal to _b_, no further shake checks will be performed. The number of times the ball shakes is the same as the number of shake checks that were performed. The table is essentially a very low-precision lookup table with numbers corresponding to the shake rate in later generations, so ultimately, aside from rounding errors (very bad ones in this case), the shake and capture rate remain similar between Generation II and the formula later used in Generation III. 
 
 ## Capture method (Generation III-IV)
 
 ### Modified catch rate
 
 The modified catch rate, _a_, is calculated in [Generation III](/wiki/Generation_III "Generation III") and [Generation IV](/wiki/Generation_IV "Generation IV") as follows: 
 
 a\=3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent3×HPmax×rate×bonusball×bonusstatus
 
 Where 
 
 *   HPmax is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at full health.
 *   HPcurrent is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at the moment.
 *   rate is the [catch rate of the Pokémon](/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon_by_catch_rate "List of Pokémon by catch rate") (which may be modified due to use of [Apricorn](/wiki/Apricorn "Apricorn") balls or actions in the [Safari Zone](/wiki/Safari_Zone "Safari Zone")).
 *   bonusball is the multiplier for the Poké Ball used.
 *   bonusstatus is the multiplier for any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") the Pokémon has (2 for sleep and freeze; 1.5 for paralysis, poison, or burn; 1 otherwise). Due to a bug in Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire, if the target Pokémon is afflicted with [bad poison](/wiki/Poison_\(status_condition\) "Poison (status condition)"), no catch bonus is applied. This was fixed in Pokémon FireRed, LeafGreen, and Emerald.
 
 If a Pokémon could have 0 HP, the maximum value for _a_ would be rate × bonusball × bonusstatus. For a Pokémon with full health and no status condition, and with a neutral ball used, the minimum value for _a_ would be rate / 3. 
 
 The formula is slightly different when applied to the [Apricorn](/wiki/Apricorn "Apricorn") balls in [Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_HeartGold_and_SoulSilver_Versions "Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver Versions"). The modifiers for these balls are applied directly to the Pokémon's catch rate, rather than in the formula. In this case, bonusball is always 1, and the catch rate cannot go higher than 255. This means that for Pokémon whose catch rate is already 255, such as [Rattata](/wiki/Rattata_\(Pok%C3%A9mon\) "Rattata (Pokémon)"), the Apricorn balls do not make the capture any more likely than a regular Poké Ball. 
 
 For [Shadow Pokémon](/wiki/Shadow_Pok%C3%A9mon "Shadow Pokémon"), their base catch rate is [determined separately](/wiki/List_of_Shadow_Pok%C3%A9mon "List of Shadow Pokémon"), usually being higher than the normal catch rate for their species. 
 
 ### Hoenn/Kanto Safari Game
 
 In Generation III, a different formula is used to calculate a Pokémon's modified catch rate during a [Safari Game](/wiki/Safari_Game "Safari Game"). The modified catch rate is calculated from the Pokémon's "catch factor". The catch factor is initialized as: 
 
 catchFactorbase\=max⁡(⌊rate12.75⌋,1)
 
 The Pokémon's catch factor can be modified by the player's actions. 
 
 *   In [Pokémon Ruby, Sapphire](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire_Versions "Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire Versions"), and [Emerald](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Emerald_Version "Pokémon Emerald Version"), going near the Pokémon increases the catch factor by 4, then 3, then 2, then 1.
 *   In [Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen_Versions "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen Versions"): bait halves the catch factor (rounding down, to a minimum of 3); rocks double the catch factor (to a maximum of 20).
 
 The modified catch rate is calculated as 
 
 a\=catchFactor×12.75
 
 As a quirk, throwing one bait at a [Chansey](/wiki/Chansey_\(Pok%C3%A9mon\) "Chansey (Pokémon)") at the start of an encounter will actually _increase_ its catch factor, as its base catch factor is 2. 
 
 ### Gr

 ### Shake checks
 
 To perform a shake check, a random[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) number between 0 and 65535 (inclusive) is generated and compared to _b_. If the number is greater than or equal to _b_, the check "fails". 
 
 Four shake checks are performed. The Pokémon is caught if all four shake checks succeed. Otherwise, the Poké Ball will shake as many times as there were successful shake checks before the Pokémon breaks free. 
 
 If a Master Ball is used, the amount of successful shake checks is set to four.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) 
 
 In [Pokémon Colosseum](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum") and [Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_XD:_Gale_of_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness"), the Pokémon breaks free after shaking once if the first or second check fails. Otherwise, the Poké Ball will shake as many times as there were successful shake checks before the Pokémon breaks free. A different message will appear depending on if the first or second check fails, despite the Poké Ball always shaking at least once. 
 
 If _a_ is 255 or greater, the capture will always succeed and no shake checks will be performed.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) 
 
 ### Probability of capture
 
 The probability _p_ of catching a Pokémon—given the values _a_ and _b_ calculated above for each shake, then requiring all 4 shakes be passed—is approximately (b65535)4, or simply a255. Due to rounding errors produced when calculating _b_, this approximation can be significantly inaccurate; for example, all _a_ values greater than 200 yield the same _b_ value, 65535, which results in a 99.994% chance of a successful capture. 
 
 For a constant capture probability _p_, the probability P(r) that a player can capture the Pokémon with no more than _r_ tries is: 
 
 P(r)=1−(1−p)r
 
 Note that this is the cumulative probability function for the [random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/random_variable "wp:random variable") r, which has a [geometric distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/geometric_distribution "wp:geometric distribution"). The [expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/expected_value "wp:expected value") of the random variable _r_ is 1/_p_, that is to say, on average, a Pokémon that can be caught with probability _p_ will be caught with 1/_p_ tries. 
 
 The inverse problem, the number of tries, _r_, needed to have a probability _P_ of capturing a Pokémon is: 
 
 r\=log⁡(1−P)log⁡(1−p)
 
 ## Capture method (Generation V)
 
 ### Modified catch rate
 
 [Generation V](/wiki/Generation_V "Generation V") follows the formula in Generation III-IV, with all divisions above either rounded down to the nearest multiple of 1/4096, or subject to standard rounding to the nearest multiple of 1/4096, rounded up at 0.5. Internally, this is represented by the modified catch rate now ranging from 0 to 1044480 (255×4096), with the HP factor 3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent above being multiplied by 4096. However, there are three alterations, and in Generation V specifically, the modified catch rate formula is: 
 
 a\=⌊3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent3×HPmax×4096×darkGrass×rate×bonusball⌋×bonusstatus×passPower
 
 *   HPmax is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at full health.
 *   HPcurrent is the number of hit points the Pokémon currently has.
 *   darkGrass only applies if the battle is taking place in [dark grass](/wiki/Dark_grass "Dark grass"), and is, as below, depending on how many Pokémon are registered as owned in the [Pokédex](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9dex "Pokédex"). Result is subject to standard rounding, rounding up at 0.5.
 
 | Number Caught | Multiplier       |
 | ------------- | ---------------- |
 | \> 600        | 1                |
 | 451-600       | 3686/4096 (~0.9) |
 | 301-450       | 3277/4096 (~0.8) |
 | 151-300       | 2867/4096 (~0.7) |
 | 30-150        | 2048/4096 (0.5)  |
 | < 30          | 1229/4096 (~0.3) |
 
 *   rate is the [catch rate of the Pokémon](/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon_by_catch_rate "List of Pokémon by catch rate").
 *   bonusball is the multiplier for the Poké Ball used. Result is subject to standard rounding, rounding up at 0.5.
 *   bonusstatus is the multiplier for any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") the Pokémon has (2.5 for sleep and freeze, 1.5 for paralyze, poison, or burn, and 1 otherwise). Notably, [sleep](/wiki/Sleep_\(status_condition\) "Sleep (status condition)") and [freeze](/wiki/Freeze_\(status_condition\) "Freeze (status condition)")'s multipliers were boosted from 2 to 2.5.
 *   passPower is 1 if no Capture [Pass Power](/wiki/Pass_Power "Pass Power") is in effect, 1.1 if Capture Power ↑ is in effect, 1.2 if Capture Power ↑↑ is in effect, or 1.3 if Capture Power ↑↑↑, S, or MAX is in effect. Result is rounded down.
 
 Some lit indoor areas will not give the [Dusk Ball](/wiki/Dusk_Ball "Dusk Ball") its boosted multiplier, even during the night. 
 
 If the modified catch rate is 1044480 or greater, the Pokémon is guaranteed to be caught (but a critical capture check will be performed anyway). 
 
 ### Shake probability
 
 The formula for _b_ is 
 
 b\=⌊65536×a10444804⌋ 
 
 ### Shake checks
 
 Generation V's shake checks work essentially the same as those of Generations III and IV. 
 
 Before any shake checks are performed, the game checks to see if a critical capture may happen. If not, three shake checks will be performed, otherwise, only one shake check will be performed. 
 
 In a normal capture, the Pokémon breaks free without shaking if the first check fails or after one shake if the second check fails. If the third check fails, the Pokémon breaks free after **three** shakes (not two). 
 
 In a critical capture, the ball will always shake once, and the Pokémon will break free or be caught depending on the result of the shake check. 
 
 ### Probability of capture
 
 In these games, the probability of catching a Pokémon (given a non-critical capture) is approximately (b65535)3, which is (a1044480)0.75. Aside from the higher-precision _a_ value, this is roughly analogous to using the shake chance from Generations III and IV but applying it three times instead of four. Before this generation, the base catch rate of a Pokémon was proportional to its probability of being captured under identical circumstances (assuming no probabilities exceed 100%).  ### Shake probability
 
 The shake probability is calculated as follows: 
 
 b\=104856016711680a 
 
 The divisions and square roots all round down to the nearest integer. 
 
 ### Shake checks
 
 To perform a shake check, a random[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) number between 0 and 65535 (inclusive) is generated and compared to _b_. If the number is greater than or equal to _b_, the check "fails". 
 
 Four shake checks are performed. The Pokémon is caught if all four shake checks succeed. Otherwise, the Poké Ball will shake as many times as there were successful shake checks before the Pokémon breaks free. 
 
 If a Master Ball is used, the amount of successful shake checks is set to four.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) 
 
 In [Pokémon Colosseum](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum") and [Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_XD:_Gale_of_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness"), the Pokémon breaks free after shaking once if the first or second check fails. Otherwise, the Poké Ball will shake as many times as there were successful shake checks before the Pokémon breaks free. A different message will appear depending on if the first or second check fails, despite the Poké Ball always shaking at least once. 
 
 If _a_ is 255 or greater, the capture will always succeed and no shake checks will be performed.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) 
 
 ### Probability of capture
 
 The probability _p_ of catching a Pokémon—given the values _a_ and _b_ calculated above for each shake, then requiring all 4 shakes be passed—is approximately (b65535)4, or simply a255. Due to rounding errors produced when calculating _b_, this approximation can be significantly inaccurate; for example, all _a_ values greater than 200 yield the same _b_ value, 65535, which results in a 99.994% chance of a successful capture. 
 
 For a constant capture probability _p_, the probability P(r) that a player can capture the Pokémon with no more than _r_ tries is: 
 
 P(r)=1−(1−p)r
 
 Note that this is the cumulative probability function for the [random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/random_variable "wp:random variable") r, which has a [geometric distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/geometric_distribution "wp:geometric distribution"). The [expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/expected_value "wp:expected value") of the random variable _r_ is 1/_p_, that is to say, on average, a Pokémon that can be caught with probability _p_ will be caught with 1/_p_ tries. 
 
 The inverse problem, the number of tries, _r_, needed to have a probability _P_ of capturing a Pokémon is: 
 
 r\=log⁡(1−P)log⁡(1−p)
 
 ## Capture method (Generation V)
 
 ### Modified catch rate
 
 [Generation V](/wiki/Generation_V "Generation V") follows the formula in Generation III-IV, with all divisions above either rounded down to the nearest multiple of 1/4096, or subject to standard rounding to the nearest multiple of 1/4096, rounded up at 0.5. Internally, this is represented by the modified catch rate now ranging from 0 to 1044480 (255×4096), with the HP factor 3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent above being multiplied by 4096. However, there are three alterations, and in Generation V specifically, the modified catch rate formula is: 
 
 a\=⌊3×HPmax−2×HPcurrent3×HPmax×4096×darkGrass×rate×bonusball⌋×bonusstatus×passPower
 
 *   HPmax is the number of hit points the Pokémon has at full health.
 *   HPcurrent is the number of hit points the Pokémon currently has.
 *   darkGrass only applies if the battle is taking place in [dark grass](/wiki/Dark_grass "Dark grass"), and is, as below, depending on how many Pokémon are registered as owned in the [Pokédex](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9dex "Pokédex"). Result is subject to standard rounding, rounding up at 0.5.
 
 | Number Caught | Multiplier       |
 | ------------- | ---------------- |
 | \> 600        | 1                |
 | 451-600       | 3686/4096 (~0.9) |
 | 301-450       | 3277/4096 (~0.8) |
 | 151-300       | 2867/4096 (~0.7) |
 | 30-150        | 2048/4096 (0.5)  |
 | < 30          | 1229/4096 (~0.3) |
 
 *   rate is the [catch rate of the Pokémon](/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon_by_catch_rate "List of Pokémon by catch rate").
 *   bonusball is the multiplier for the Poké Ball used. Result is subject to standard rounding, rounding up at 0.5.
 *   bonusstatus is the multiplier for any [status condition](/wiki/Status_condition "Status condition") the Pokémon has (2.5 for sleep and freeze, 1.5 for paralyze, poison, or burn, and 1 otherwise). Notably, [sleep](/wiki/Sleep_\(status_condition\) "Sleep (status condition)") and [freeze](/wiki/Freeze_\(status_condition\) "Freeze (status condition)")'s multipliers were boosted from 2 to 2.5.
 *   passPower is 1 if no Capture [Pass Power](/wiki/Pass_Power "Pass Power") is in effect, 1.1 if Capture Power ↑ is in effect, 1.2 if Capture Power ↑↑ is in effect, or 1.3 if Capture Power ↑↑↑, S, or MAX is in effect. Result is rounded down.
 
 Some lit indoor areas will not give the [Dusk Ball](/wiki/Dusk_Ball "Dusk Ball") its boosted multiplier, even during the night. 
 
 If the modified catch rate is 1044480 or greater, the Pokémon is guaranteed to be caught (but a critical capture check will be performed anyway). 
 
 ### Shake probability
 
 The formula for _b_ is 
 
 b\=⌊65536×a10444804⌋ 
 
 ### Shake checks
 
 Generation V's shake checks work essentially the same as those of Generations III and IV. 
 
 Before any shake checks are performed, the game checks to see if a critical capture may happen. If not, three shake checks will be performed, otherwise, only one shake check will be performed. 
 
 In a normal capture, the Pokémon breaks free without shaking if the first check fails or after one shake if the second check fails. If the third check fails, the Pokémon breaks free after **three** shakes (not two). 
 
 In a critical capture, the ball will always shake once, and the Pokémon will break free or be caught depending on the result of the shake check. 
 
 ### Probability of capture
 
 In these games, the probability of catching a Pokémon (given a non-critical capture) is approximately (b65535)3, which is (a1044480)0.75. Aside from the higher-precision _a_ value, this is roughly analogous to using the shake chance from Generations III and IV but applying it three times instead of four. Before this generation, the base catch rate of a Pokémon was proportional to its probability of being captured under identical circumstances (assuming no probabilities exceed 100%). This stops being the case starting from [Pokémon Black and White](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Black_and_White_Versions "Pokémon Black and White Versions"), where _a_ now corresponds to the capture probability raised to the power of 43 (which makes the probability higher for a given value of _a_).

### Effect

#### Manual activation

When used from the [Bag](/wiki/Bag "Bag") in a [wild](/wiki/Wild_Pok%C3%A9mon "Wild Pokémon") encounter, it attempts to catch the wild Pokémon. If used on the first turn of the encounter, it has an increased [catch rate](/wiki/Catch_rate "Catch rate") modifier. 

The Quick Ball cannot be used in situations in which Poké Balls cannot be used, such as in wild battles with two or more opponents currently present or against a [trial](/wiki/Island_challenge "Island challenge") Pokémon. If used in a Trainer battle, the opposing Trainer will deflect the ball, wasting the player's turn. 

#### Generation IV

If used on the first turn of the encounter, the Quick Ball has a 4× [catch rate](/wiki/Catch_rate "Catch rate") modifier; otherwise, it has a 1× modifier. 

#### Generation V onward

If used on the first turn of the encounter, the Quick Ball has a 5× [catch rate](/wiki/Catch_rate "Catch rate") modifier; otherwise, it has a 1× modifier. If used on an [Ultra Beast](/wiki/Ultra_Beast "Ultra Beast"), the catch rate modifier is instead always set to 410/4096× (~0.1×). 

In [Pokémon Legends: Z-A](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Legends:_Z-A "Pokémon Legends: Z-A"), the bonus is instead applied if neither the wild Pokémon nor the player's active Pokémon have used any moves since the beginning of the battle. Furthermore, the bonus is now only 3×. 

#### Held item

[Fling](/wiki/Fling_\(move\) "Fling (move)") fails if the user is holding a Quick Ball.

# Animated

The `Animated` library is designed to make animations fluid, powerful, and painless to build and maintain. `Animated` focuses on declarative relationships between inputs and outputs, configurable transforms in between, and `start`/`stop` methods to control time-based animation execution.

The core workflow for creating an animation is to create an `Animated.Value`, hook it up to one or more style attributes of an animated component, and then drive updates via animations using `Animated.timing()`.

There are two value types you can use with `Animated`:

*   [`Animated.Value()`](/docs/animated#value) for single values
*   [`Animated.ValueXY()`](/docs/animated#valuexy) for vectors

`Animated.Value` can bind to style properties or other props, and can be interpolated as well. A single `Animated.Value` can drive any number of properties.

### Configuring animations[​](#configuring-animations "Direct link to Configuring animations")

`Animated` provides three types of animation types. Each animation type provides a particular animation curve that controls how your values animate from their initial value to the final value:

*   [`Animated.decay()`](/docs/animated#decay) starts with an initial velocity and gradually slows to a stop.
*   [`Animated.spring()`](/docs/animated#spring) provides a basic spring physics model.
*   [`Animated.timing()`](/docs/animated#timing) animates a value over time using [easing functions](/docs/easing).

In most cases, you will be using `timing()`. By default, it uses a symmetric easeInOut curve that conveys the gradual acceleration of an object to full speed and concludes by gradually decelerating to a stop.

### Working with animations[​](#working-with-animations "Direct link to Working with animations")

Animations are started by calling `start()` on your animation. `start()` takes a completion callback that will be called when the animation is done. If the animation finished running normally, the completion callback will be invoked with `{finished: true}`. If the animation is done because `stop()` was called on it before it could finish (e.g. because it was interrupted by a gesture or another animation), then it will receive `{finished: false}`.

Only animatable components can be animated. These unique components do the magic of binding the animated values to the properties, and do targeted native updates to avoid the cost of the React render and reconciliation process on every frame. *   [`createAnimatedComponent()`](/docs/animated#createanimatedcomponent) can be used to make a component animatable.

It can be used to catch a [wild Pokémon](/wiki/Wild_Pok%C3%A9mon "Wild Pokémon"), being more likely to succeed the longer it has been since the start of the [battle](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_battle "Pokémon battle"). It was developed by the [Devon Corporation](/wiki/Devon_Corporation "Devon Corporation").

### Effect

When used from the [Bag](/wiki/Bag "Bag") in a [wild](/wiki/Wild_Pok%C3%A9mon "Wild Pokémon") encounter, it attempts to catch the wild Pokémon. It has an increased catch rate modifier in certain encounters. 

The Dive Ball cannot be used in situations in which Poké Balls cannot be used, such as in wild battles with two or more opponents currently present or against a [trial](/wiki/Island_challenge "Island challenge") Pokémon. If used in a Trainer b

attle (except if used as a [Snag Ball](/wiki/Snag_Ball "Snag Ball") on a [Shadow Pokémon](/wiki/Shadow_Pok%C3%A9mon "Shadow Pokémon")), the opposing Trainer will deflect the ball, wasting the item. If used on the [ghost Marowak](/wiki/Marowak_\(ghost\) "Marowak (ghost)"), it will dodge the ball, wasting it. 

#### Generation III

If used [underwater](/wiki/Underwater "Underwater"), the Dive Ball has a 3.5× [catch rate](/wiki/Catch_rate "Catch rate") modifier; otherwise, it has a 1× modifier. Since there are no underwater areas in [Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen_Versions "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen Versions"), it will always have a 1× modifier in those games. In [Pokémon Colosseum](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum") and [Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_XD:_Gale_of_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness"), [Phenac Stadium](/wiki/Phenac_Stadium "Phenac Stadium") is considered an underwater area, so the Dive Ball has a 3.5× catch rate modifier there. 

#### Generation IV to VIII

If used while [surfing](/wiki/Surf_\(move\) "Surf (move)"), [fishing](/wiki/Fishing "Fishing"), or [underwater](/wiki/Underwater "Underwater"), the Dive Ball has a 3.5× [catch rate](/wiki/Catch_rate "Catch rate") modifier; otherwise, it has a 1× modifier. If used on an [Ultra Beast](/wiki/Ultra_Beast "Ultra Beast"), the catch rate modifier is instead always set to 410/4096× (~0.1×). 

#### Generation IX

If used while the Pokémon is currently on or in water, the Dive Ball has a 3.5× [catch rate](/wiki/Catch_rate "Catch rate") modifier; otherwise, it has a 1× modifier. The bonus catch rate only applies to Pokémon that swim in water, or typically walk on land and have entered water. 

Pokémon that always fly or hover do not benefit from this bonus, excluding instances where a Pokémon typically walks on land, but has an animation of "flying over water" instead of "swimming in water", such as [Tropius](/wiki/Tropius_\(Pok%C3%A9mon\) "Tropius (Pokémon)").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) 

Additionally, the pool of water near the [Firescourge Shrine](/wiki/Firescourge_Shrine "Firescourge Shrine") is not properly considered "water" due to a bug, and therefore nothing benefits from an increased catch rate from Dive Balls there, even if the Pokémon would otherwise be eligible.

Contents of https://reactnative.dev/docs/scrollview:
# ScrollView

Component that wraps platform ScrollView while providing integration with touch locking "responder" system.

Keep in mind that ScrollViews must have a bounded height in order to work, since they contain unbounded-height children into a bounded container (via a scroll interaction). In order to bound the height of a ScrollView, either set the height of the view directly (discouraged) or make sure all parent views have bounded height. Forgetting to transfer `{flex: 1}` down the view stack can lead to errors here, which the element inspector makes quick to debug.

Doesn't yet support other contained responders from blocking this scroll view from becoming the responder.

`<ScrollView>` vs [`<FlatList>`](/docs/flatlist) - which one to use?

`ScrollView` renders all its react child components at once, but this has a performance downside.

Imagine you have a very long list of items you want to display, maybe several screens worth of content. Creating JS components and native views for everything all at once, much of which may not even be shown, will contribute to slow rendering and increased memory usage.

This is where `FlatList` comes into play. `FlatList` renders items lazily, when they are about to appear, and removes items that scroll way off screen to save memory and processing time.

`FlatList` is also handy if you want to render separators between your items, multiple columns, infinite scroll loading, or any number of other features it supports out of the box.

# Animated

The `Animated` library is designed to make animations fluid, powerful, and painless to build and maintain. `Animated` focuses on declarative relationships between inputs and outputs, configurable transforms in between, and `start`/`stop` methods to control time-based animation execution.

The core workflow for creating an animation is to create an `Animated.Value`, hook it up to one or more style attributes of an animated component, and then drive updates via animations using `Animated.timing()`.

note

Don't modify the animated value directly. You can use the [`useRef` Hook](https://react.dev/reference/react/useRef) to return a mutable ref object. This ref object's `current` property is initialized as the given argument and persists throughout the component lifecycle.

## Example[​](#example "Direct link to Example")

Refer to the [Animations](/docs/animations#animated-api) guide to see additional examples of `Animated` in action.

## Overview[​](#overview "Direct link to Overview")

There are two value types you can use with `Animated`:

*   [`Animated.Value()`](/docs/animated#value) for single values
*   [`Animated.ValueXY()`](/docs/animated#valuexy) for vectors

`Animated.Value` can bind to style properties or other props, and can be interpolated as well. A single `Animated.Value` can drive any number of properties.

### Configuring animations[​](#configuring-animations "Direct link to Configuring animations")

`Animated` provides three types of animation types. Each animation type provides a particular animation curve that controls how your values animate from their initial value to the final value:

*   [`Animated.decay()`](/docs/animated#decay) starts with an initial velocity and gradually slows to a stop.
*   [`Animated.spring()`](/docs/animated#spring) provides a basic spring physics model.
*   [`Animated.timing()`](/docs/animated#timing) animates a value over time using [easing functions](/docs/easing).

In most cases, you will be using `timing()`. By default, it uses a symmetric easeInOut curve that conveys the gradual acceleration of an object to full speed and concludes by gradually decelerating to a stop.

### Working with animations[​](#working-with-animations "Direct link to Working with animations")

Animations are started by calling `start()` on your animation. `start()` takes a completion callback that will be called when the animation is done. If the animation finished running normally, the completion callback will be invoked with `{finished: true}`. If the animation is done because `stop()` was called on it before it could finish (e.g. because it was interrupted by a gesture or another animation), then it will receive `{finished: false}`.

React TSX

```tsx


Animated.timing({}).start(({finished}) => {



  /* completion callback */



});

```

### Using the native driver[​](#using-the-native-driver "Direct link to Using the native driver")

By using the native driver, we send everything about the animation to native before starting the animation, allowing native code to perform the animation on the UI thread without having to go through the bridge on every frame. Once the animation has started, the JS thread can be blocked without affecting the animation.

You can use the native driver by specifying `useNativeDriver: true` in your animation configuration. See the [Animations](/docs/animations#using-the-native-driver) guide to learn more.

### Animatable components[​](#animatable-components "Direct link to Animatable components")

Only animatable components can be animated. These unique components do the magic of binding the animated values to the properties, and do targeted native updates to avoid the cost of the React render and reconciliation process on every frame. They also handle cleanup on unmount so they are safe by default.

*   [`createAnimatedComponent()`](/docs/animated#createanimatedcomponent) can be used to make a component animatable.

`Animated` exports the following animatable components using the above wrapper:

*   `Animated.Image`
*   `Animated.ScrollView`
*   `Animated.Text`
*   `Animated.View`
*   `Animated.FlatList`
*   `Animated.SectionList`

## The short version

I added a **catching simulator** to the Pokémon detail flow. You choose a game ruleset, a Poké Ball, and encounter conditions. The screen estimates the chance for that throw, then animates a ball toward the Pokémon and shows whether it was caught.

The word *simulator* matters: it **does not save a Pokémon** or change your Pokédex. It simulates an individual throw using the available data and modeled game rules.

## What happens, step by step

1. **The screen reads the Pokémon choice** from the route, including its form and whether it should use a shiny sprite. It loads the appearance, Pokémon details, and ball data through TanStack Query, which caches the results. See [the screen’s data loading](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/app/pokemon/simulator/[id].tsx:150>) and [the API service](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/services/pokemon-api.ts:422>).

2. **The screen shows the encounter first.** The Pokémon sprite, chance, throw button, and outcome now live together. The Poké Balls are in a horizontal carousel; the selected ball’s description appears beneath it. The layout and encounter scene are in [the simulator screen](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/app/pokemon/simulator/[id].tsx:368>).

3. **Your controls change the chance.** You can change remaining HP, status, time of day where supported, and water or fishing conditions. The code combines those choices into a `conditions` value, then uses it to calculate the displayed chance.

4. **Tapping Throw starts the simulation.** The ball animates toward the Pokémon. After it reaches the sprite, the simulator rolls against the calculated probability. If successful, the sprite shrinks into the ball; otherwise, the Pokémon breaks free. The throw flow is in [the `throwBall` function](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/app/pokemon/simulator/[id].tsx:249>).

## A small probability example

The rule code returns a number between `0` and `1`. For example, `0.0588` is shown as **5.88%**.

```ts
const caught = Math.random() < catchChance;
```

That means each throw has the displayed chance of succeeding. A 5.88% chance does **not** mean it will catch the Pokémon after a particular number of tries. It might succeed early, or take many throws. A Master Ball is modeled as a guaranteed catch.

The calculation is in [the catch-rules module](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/services/pokemon-catching-rules.ts:229>). It accounts for modeled ball effects, HP, status, and supported encounter conditions.

## Why some choices are disabled

Catch rules vary between games, and some balls need information the screen doesn’t ask for. For example, a Nest Ball needs the wild Pokémon’s level; a Timer Ball needs elapsed turns. Rather than guess, the simulator disables those balls and explains why.

Only Generation III and IV rulesets are modeled. Other games with unsupported catch systems aren’t offered as if their results were accurate. That choice is handled by [ruleset and ball availability checks](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/services/pokemon-catching-rules.ts:73>).

One visual limitation: **the animated ball is currently a generic Poké Ball**, even when you select a different ball. The selected ball affects the chance, but its artwork isn’t shown in the animation yet.

## How this relates to the checklist you highlighted

- **Live data through TanStack Query:** used to load Pokémon and Poké Ball data.
- **Loading and error state on every load:** the simulator has loading indicators and retry messages for its data requests.
- **TypeScript and ESLint:** the checks passed after the changes.
- **SQLite that survives a restart:** not added; simulated catches aren’t saved.
- **UI, data, and logic in separate files:** API data handling and catch rules are in separate service files. The simulator screen still contains its own UI and screen state.

The main files are [the simulator screen](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/app/pokemon/simulator/[id].tsx>), [the PokéAPI service](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/services/pokemon-api.ts>), [the catch-rules module](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/services/pokemon-catching-rules.ts>), and [its focused tests](</C:/Inholland/Jaar 4/Application Design and Development/Frontend Development/React-Native-Final-Assignment-Pokedex/src/services/pokemon-catching-rules.test.ts>).
